content.overview: Liability of the State for torts of its servants was historically limited by a sovereign/non-sovereign distinction (Kasturi Lal). Modern public-law compensation for violation of fundamental rights under Articles 32 and 226 (Rudul Sah, Nilabati Behera, D.K. Basu) substantially undercuts immunity rhetoric where constitutional rights are breached.

sections.heading: Sovereign and non-sovereign functions
sections.body: Kasturi Lal reflected a narrow approach to State liability for police-related loss in the exercise of sovereign powers. Later jurisprudence emphasises accountability and rights-based compensation.

sections.heading: Constitutional torts
sections.body: Illegal detention, custodial violence, and similar State wrongs attract public-law damages to vindicate fundamental rights. Compensation is not merely private tort damages by another name; it is a public-law remedy.

learningObjectives: Understand the constitutional and common-law basis of State liability in tort under Article 300 of the Constitution of India.

Trace the historical evolution of the sovereign-function defence from P&O Steam Navigation and Kasturi Lal to its dramatic narrowing in N. Nagendra Rao and Achutrao Haribhau Khodwa ((1996) 2 SCC 634).
Differentiate ordinary private-law tort damages under Section 9 CPC from public-law constitutional compensation under Articles 32 and 226 for fundamental rights infringements.

Analyze the landmark ruling in Chairman, Railway Board v. Chandrima Das ((2000) 2 SCC 465) on commercial undertakings, non-citizen rights under Article 21, and State vicarious liability in public law.
enhancement.definition: State liability in tort concerns the legal accountability of the Union of India or a State Government for wrongful or negligent acts committed by its public officers, servants, or instrumentalities, encompassing both ordinary civil suits for unliquidated damages under Article 300 and public-law compensation under Articles 32 and 226 for infringements of fundamental rights.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Under Article 300 of the Constitution, the Union of India and State Governments may sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in like cases as the Dominion of India and corresponding Provinces might have sued or been sued prior to the Constitution. The historical immunity recognized in Kasturi Lal (1965) for acts done in exercise of sovereign powers has been substantially confined by the Supreme Court in Achutrao Haribhau Khodwa ((1996) 2 SCC 634) and N. Nagendra Rao ((1994) 6 SCC 205) exclusively to core inalienable functions of a constitutional government (defence, foreign affairs, administration of justice, maintenance of public order). Welfare activities (running hospitals) and commercial operations (railway transit) do not enjoy sovereign immunity. Where fundamental rights (especially Article 21) are infringed, public-law compensation is awarded independently of private-law sovereign immunity defences (Chandrima Das, Nilabati Behera, Rudul Sah).
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Constitution of India (Article 300 for suits by and against Union/States, Articles 21, 32, and 226 for fundamental rights and constitutional torts, Article 372 for continuity of laws); Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Sections 79-82, Order XXVII for suits by/against Government, Section 80 for mandatory 2-month statutory notice); Limitation Act, 1963 (Articles 112 and 113); Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 for proof of official acts.
essentialIngredients: 1. Jural Act of Public Servant: The impugned act or omission must be committed by an officer, servant, or agency of the Union or a State in the course of public employment.

2. Actionable Tort or Fundamental Right Infringement: The conduct must amount to an actionable civil wrong (negligence, false imprisonment, trespass) or an egregious violation of guaranteed constitutional rights (especially Article 21).

3. Non-Sovereign Character for Private Law: In ordinary private-law tort suits under Article 300, the activity must not be an inalienable primary sovereign function; welfare, commercial, and administrative services carry ordinary employer vicarious liability (Achutrao Khodwa).

4. Inapplicability of Sovereign Immunity to Constitutional Torts: In writ proceedings under Articles 32/226, sovereign immunity is wholly inapplicable where State agents violate fundamental human rights (Chandrima Das).

5. Compliance with Procedural Preconditions: In private-law suits, service of statutory notice under Section 80 CPC is mandatory unless leave to sue without notice is granted under Section 80(2) CPC for urgent relief.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Liability of the State for torts of its servants was historically limited by a sovereign/non-sovereign distinction (Kasturi Lal). Modern public-law compensation for violation of fundamental rights under Articles 32 and 226 (Rudul Sah, Nilabati Behera, D.K. Basu) substantially undercuts immunity rhetoric where constitutional rights are breached.

Sovereign and non-sovereign functions
Kasturi Lal reflected a narrow approach to State liability for police-related loss in the exercise of sovereign powers. Later jurisprudence emphasises accountability and rights-based compensation.

Constitutional torts
Illegal detention, custodial violence, and similar State wrongs attract public-law damages to vindicate fundamental rights. Compensation is not merely private tort damages by another name; it is a public-law remedy.

Track B
Choose the correct path: civil suit against the State/officials and/or writ petition with compensation prayer. Plead constitutional violations with facts of State action. Do not treat Kasturi Lal as the last word without checking the rights-based line of cases.

In Achutrao Haribhau Khodwa v. State of Maharashtra ((1996) 2 SCC 634), the Supreme Court reviewed Vidhyawati and Kasturi Lal, affirming that running a civil hospital is a welfare activity and not an immune sovereign function. Barring core inalienable functions such as defence and administration of justice, the State is vicariously liable for tortious negligence of its employees.

In Chairman, Railway Board v. Chandrima Das ((2000) 2 SCC 465), the Supreme Court held that the Union running railways is engaged in a commercial activity with no sovereign immunity, and affirmed that public-law compensation under Article 226 is available to non-citizens whose fundamental rights to bodily integrity under Article 21 are violated by State employees.
examples: Illustration 1 — Medical Negligence in State Hospital (Private Law): Surviving family members of a patient who died due to surgical negligence (leaving a mop inside the peritoneal cavity) in a government civil hospital file a civil suit for damages against the State under Article 300. The State cannot plead sovereign immunity because running a hospital is a welfare function; the State is vicariously liable in damages (Achutrao Haribhau Khodwa).

Illustration 2 — Custodial / Premises Tort Infringing Article 21 (Constitutional Tort): A foreign national is subjected to sexual assault by public employees inside a railway transit facility. An advocate files a writ petition under Article 226 claiming compensation. Sovereign immunity is unavailable; the High Court and Supreme Court award monetary compensation in public law against the Union for violation of Article 21 (Chandrima Das).
enhancement.problemApplication:
Problem: A citizen's vehicle is damaged, and their minor passenger injured, through the rash and negligent driving of a government vehicle operated by an administrative officer returning from a routine welfare inspection. The State claims sovereign immunity under Article 300, citing Kasturi Lal.

Application & Assessment: (1) Under State of Rajasthan v. Mst. Vidhyawati (AIR 1962 SC 933) and Achutrao Haribhau Khodwa ((1996) 2 SCC 634), the State is liable for torts committed by its servants in the course of employment just like any ordinary employer, unless the act was in discharge of an inalienable primary sovereign function (e.g. warfare, maintaining public order, repressing crime). (2) Routine administrative or welfare travel is not an inalienable sovereign function. (3) The State cannot claim immunity and is vicariously liable in damages to the vehicle owner and the injured passenger (acting through their next friend under Order XXXII CPC).
keyTakeaways: State liability under Article 300: The State is vicariously liable for torts of its employees acting within the scope of employment, except in core inalienable sovereign functions (Vidhyawati, Achutrao Khodwa).

Erosion of Kasturi Lal: In a welfare state, activities such as running hospitals, public transport, or commercial services are not sovereign functions; sovereign immunity cannot defeat actionable negligence claims.

Constitutional torts: Public-law compensation under Articles 32 and 226 operates to redress fundamental rights violations (especially Article 21) independent of private-law sovereign immunity (Chandrima Das, Nilabati Behera).
Procedural preconditions: Private civil suits require Section 80 CPC notice; writ petitions for constitutional tort compensation do not require statutory notice.

distinctions.title: Private-law tort suit under Article 300 versus Public-law constitutional compensation under Articles 32/226
distinctions.left: Private-law tort suit: Ordinary civil action instituted under Section 9 CPC in accordance with Article 300; requires adherence to Section 80 CPC notice and statutory limitation.
distinctions.right: Constitutional compensation: Summary public-law remedy awarded by Supreme Court (Art. 32) or High Courts (Art. 226) to redress egregious infringements of fundamental rights (especially Article 21); independent of strict private-law pleading rules.

rows.right: Public-law compensation for infringement of fundamental rights

rows.left: Formal plaint, strict civil proof, and Section 80 CPC notice
rows.right: Writ petition, broad probabilities, and vindication of constitutional rights

distinctions.title: Sovereign functions versus Welfare / Commercial functions of the State
distinctions.left: Sovereign functions: Inalienable primary governmental functions such as defence, maintenance of law and order, and administration of justice where immunity was historically recognized under strict Kasturi Lal line.
distinctions.right: Welfare / Commercial functions: Running passenger transport, civil hospitals, or public amenities where the State possesses no immunity and is liable as an ordinary employer (Achutrao Haribhau Khodwa, Chandrima Das).

rows.left: Confined to primary inalienable sovereign functions
rows.right: No sovereign immunity; State is vicariously answerable

shortAnswer: Define State liability in tort and cite Article 300.
State the difference between sovereign and welfare functions under Achutrao Haribhau Khodwa.
Explain constitutional tort under Articles 32/226 citing Chandrima Das.
tenMark: Introduction: Constitutional basis of State liability under Article 300.
Historical background: P&O Steam Navigation, Vidhyawati, and Kasturi Lal sovereign-immunity doctrine.
Narrowing of sovereign immunity: Welfare activities (Achutrao Khodwa) and commercial operations (Chandrima Das).
Constitutional tort: Development of public-law compensation for Article 21 violations (Rudul Sah, Nilabati Behera).
Conclusion: Evolution from colonial sovereign immunity to modern constitutional accountability.
sixteenMark: Introduction and constitutional architecture: Article 300, pre-Constitution position, and Section 79 CPC.
Judicial evolution of sovereign immunity: Detailed comparison of State of Rajasthan v. Vidhyawati and Kasturi Lal Ralia Ram Jain.
The modern welfare state transition: Critical analysis of N. Nagendra Rao and Achutrao Haribhau Khodwa ((1996) 2 SCC 634) restricting immunity to primary inalienable functions.
Emergence of constitutional tort: Remedial jurisprudence under Articles 32 and 226 for custodial deaths, illegal detention, and bodily violation.
In-depth study of Chairman, Railway Board v. Chandrima Das ((2000) 2 SCC 465): Standing, rights of non-citizens under Article 21, and vicarious liability of the Union in public law.
Procedural and remedial comparison: Private-law damages vs public-law compensation, Section 80 CPC notice requirements, and limitation considerations.
Conclusion and analysis of the Law Commission's proposals for statutory codification of State liability.

caseLaw.name: Achutrao Haribhau Khodwa v. State of Maharashtra
caseLaw.holding: Judgment dated 20/02/1996. The Supreme Court reversed the Bombay High Court and held that the State is vicariously liable in tort for the negligence of its medical officers in a government-run hospital. The Court reviewed Vidhyawati and Kasturi Lal, affirming that running a civil hospital is a welfare activity and not an immune sovereign function. Barring core inalienable functions (defence, justice administration, crime repression), the State is vicariously answerable for tortious acts of its employees.
caseLaw.relevance: Direct Supreme Court authority establishing that running a hospital is a non-sovereign welfare function for which the State is liable in tort under Article 300.

caseLaw.name: The Chairman, Railway Board v. Mrs. Chandrima Das
caseLaw.holding: Judgment dated 28/01/2000. The Supreme Court held that the Union running railways is engaged in a commercial activity with no sovereign immunity, and affirmed that public-law compensation under Article 226 is available to redress violations of fundamental rights under Article 21 committed against non-citizens by State employees.
caseLaw.relevance: Direct Supreme Court authority establishing the vicarious liability of the State in public law and the award of constitutional compensation for fundamental rights infringements.
